title: Milton Keynes City Council and Valon: streamlining planning with AI
summary: Milton Keynes reports faster validation and decisions during its Valon pilot, with receipt-to-validation time falling from 15.8 to 7.6 days.
account: Milton Keynes piloted Valon for planning work from October to December 2025. The council reports that officers validated applications 60–80% faster. Its analysis of the planning register put average receipt-to-validation time at 15.8 days before and 7.6 days during the pilot, and validation-to-decision time at 53.1 and 43.2 days. The estimated 1,360 officer hours per year is an extrapolation from an assumed 80% saving. Valon’s own account describes major-application checks falling from about 65 to 10 minutes and non-major checks from 15 to 5 minutes. It reports 7.7 days for early-November validation turnaround and a separate 18% decision-time difference against a non-pilot group. The two accounts do not publish the underlying timesheets, selected application records, sample sizes, or rules for constructing the comparisons. These are reported efficiency gains, with uncertainty about how much AI caused. The council purchased a one-year license after the pilot and reports continued use.
purpose: Support planning officers from application validation through decision-making.

ratings.reason: The council and developer report shorter validation and decision-processing times. The underlying samples and comparison methods are not published, so the gain remains a first-party estimate.
Officers report less processing work, and the council reports shorter waits for applicants. No improvement in decision quality or realized housing delivery is demonstrated.

ai_role.statement: The council used Valon to read and check planning documents and present information for officer review. The council and developer describe shorter processing times, but provide no reproducible analysis that isolates AI from case mix, staffing, or other workflow changes. Planning decisions remain officers’ responsibility.

evidence.citation: Milton Keynes City Council, “Milton Keynes City Council and Valon: streamlining planning with AI,” Local Government Association, May 8, 2026, “Impact,” “Key takeaways,” and “What’s next.”

claim_lineage.claim: The developer gives 7.7 days for early-November turnaround and an 18% difference in decision time against a non-pilot control group.

source_chain.locator: “Impact at a Glance” and “Department-Wide Velocity,” including the early-October/early-November comparison
source_chain.role: Developer’s description of comparison periods and comparator

limitations: The developer’s 7.7 differs from the LGA account’s 7.6; the sources do not explain whether the difference reflects rounding or a different window.
The claimed non-pilot control group is not defined, and comparability is not demonstrated.
An 18% difference is not interchangeable with the separate promotional claim of 18 days saved.

claim_lineage.claim: The council obtained a one-year license and continued using Valon after the pilot.
limitations: No procurement document is linked. Arcus integration is being scoped, and full rollout remains a future objective.

excluded_republications.relationship: Earlier contributor publicity repeats pilot figures and quotes the vendor CEO without providing independent evaluation or underlying records. Retained separately for chronology.

Later original reporting attributes the eight-day improvement to the council and adds broader housing-policy interviews. It supplies no new evidence about the Milton Keynes pilot’s measured effect. Generic policy context is not counted as AI-result corroboration.

limitations: The council and developer accounts are original but interested-party sources. Neither independently validates AI-caused improvements.

Neither retained page links the underlying timesheets, selected register extract, evaluation protocol, statistical analysis, appendices, or supplementary results. Those underlying materials were not inspected.
The 60–80% reported saving in officer time, the 80% assumption for annual hours, elapsed processing times, and the 18% control comparison describe different measures and are not combined.
The developer’s 7.7-day figure and the council account’s 7.6-day figure remain distinct; no unsupported reconciliation is introduced.
No source demonstrates that faster processing produced more homes or better planning decisions.
